reference.source: Cummings Otolaryngology / Emery's Principles of Medical Genetics
clinicalPearls: An auditory-pigmentary syndrome combining sensorineural hearing loss with pigmentary anomalies of the eyes, hair and skin
Characteristic features include heterochromia or brilliant blue irides, a white forelock, patchy skin depigmentation, and early greying
Dystopia canthorum (lateral displacement of the inner canthi) distinguishes type 1 from type 2, in which it is absent
Most commonly autosomal dominant with variable expressivity; PAX3 underlies types 1 and 3, and MITF and SOX10 are associated with type 2
Type 3 (Klein-Waardenburg) adds musculoskeletal limb abnormalities, and type 4 (Waardenburg-Shah) is associated with Hirschsprung disease via SOX10, EDN3 or EDNRB
Hearing loss is congenital, non-progressive and may be unilateral or bilateral, reflecting absence of melanocytes in the stria vascularis
Family examination frequently reveals affected relatives with subtle pigmentary signs
reference.pathophysiology: Waardenburg syndrome arises from mutations affecting the development, migration or survival of neural-crest-derived melanocytes. Melanocytes contribute pigment to the skin, hair and iris and are also essential within the stria vascularis of the cochlea for maintaining the endolymphatic environment needed for normal hearing. Genes such as PAX3, MITF and SOX10 encode transcription factors within this developmental pathway, so their disruption produces both the pigmentary abnormalities and the sensorineural hearing loss. In type 4 the same neural-crest defect also affects enteric ganglion cells, causing aganglionic megacolon (Hirschsprung disease).
additionalDifferentials: Other syndromic sensorineural hearing loss such as Pendred or branchio-oto-renal syndrome
Piebaldism (KIT mutation) with depigmentation but without hearing loss
Vitiligo and other acquired pigmentary disorders
Tietz syndrome with generalised hypopigmentation and deafness
Hirschsprung disease from non-syndromic causes in type 4 presentations
additionalInvestigations: Audiometry with age-appropriate testing to characterise hearing loss
Detailed dermatological and ophthalmic examination for pigmentary features and iris colour
Measurement of inner canthal and interpupillary distances to assess dystopia canthorum
Assessment for constipation or bowel obstruction and Hirschsprung disease in suspected type 4
Molecular genetic testing (PAX3, MITF, SOX10 and related genes) to confirm subtype
redFlags: Neonatal bowel obstruction or severe constipation suggesting associated Hirschsprung disease
Bilateral profound hearing loss affecting speech development in an infant
Progressive rather than static hearing loss, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Family history of combined pigmentary and hearing anomalies indicating dominant inheritance
reference.prognosis: Hearing loss is congenital and generally non-progressive, and prognosis is favourable with hearing aids or cochlear implantation and early language support; the pigmentary features are cosmetic, though associated Hirschsprung disease in type 4 requires surgical management.
pitfalls: Overlooking subtle pigmentary signs when hearing loss is the presenting problem
Confusing dystopia canthorum with true hypertelorism and misclassifying the subtype
Assuming normal hearing in one ear excludes the syndrome, as loss may be unilateral
Failing to consider Hirschsprung disease in a neonate with pigmentary features
